client: I've been having a really hard time since my dad passed away about two months ago. I can't seem to focus at work at all — I'll sit down to do something simple and my mind just goes completely blank, or I end up staring at nothing for an hour. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I'd give this a shot.
therapist: Thank you for taking that step and reaching out — losing your father is one of the most profound losses a person can experience, and what you're describing with the blank mind and difficulty focusing makes complete sense as part of grief. I also hear a kind of quiet exhaustion underneath your words, like you're carrying something very heavy but aren't sure there's any relief in sight. What would it mean for you if talking *did* help, even just a little?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I guess if talking helped even a little, it would mean I'm not just... stuck like this forever. But honestly, I'm not sure I believe that's possible right now — it feels like the grief is just baked into everything, like it's become part of the air I breathe. I don't know if words can really touch something that feels this big.
therapist: The way you describe it — grief becoming part of the air itself — is such a vivid and honest picture of how consuming this kind of loss can be, and it makes sense that words might feel inadequate in the face of something so vast. I notice there's something quietly fragile in how you're sharing this, like you're holding it very carefully, almost gently. I'm curious — when you imagine being "unstuck," even faintly, what does that look like to you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I think when I imagine being "unstuck"... it's almost like I can't fully picture it, which is part of what scares me. The closest I get is maybe just being able to sit in a room without feeling like I have to brace myself against something invisible. But even saying that out loud feels a little like I'm betraying the grief somehow, like moving forward means I'm okay with what happened, and I'm not sure I'll ever be okay with it.
therapist: What you just named — that moving forward feels like a betrayal — is one of the most common and painful knots in grief, and it's so important that you said it out loud. I want to gently offer a reframe: wanting relief from pain isn't the same as being okay with losing him, and it doesn't mean you love him any less. What do you think *he* would have wanted for you, in terms of how you carry this?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me knows you're right... but it's not that simple. When I try to imagine what he would have wanted for me, I just feel this wave of guilt, like I'm putting words in his mouth to make myself feel better. And honestly, it almost feels manipulative, like I'm using him to give myself permission to stop hurting.
therapist: The guilt you're describing — feeling like you'd be manipulating his memory just by imagining his care for you — tells me how much integrity you're bringing to this grief, but it also sounds like an incredibly exhausting standard to hold yourself to. I'm wondering if the guilt itself has become a way of staying close to him, like as long as it hurts this much, the connection remains real and intact. Does that resonate at all with how it feels?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: That actually... hit something I wasn't expecting. Like, I hadn't thought of it that way, but there's something uncomfortably true about it — if I let go of the guilt, maybe it feels like I'm letting go of him too, like the pain is proof that he mattered. But I also don't know if I fully trust that interpretation, because it almost sounds too neat, like a therapist thing to say that wraps it up in a bow, and my situation feels messier than that.
therapist: Your pushback is actually really valuable here — you're right that grief is messy, and I don't want to hand you a tidy explanation that flattens what you're actually living through. What feels true and what feels "too neat" can coexist, and it's worth sitting with the part that *did* hit something, without forcing it to mean more than it does right now. What's the messier part that you feel that framing doesn't quite capture?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I think the messier part is that I don't just miss her, I'm angry at her, and that feels awful to admit out loud. Like, she was my best friend and she just... stopped reaching out, and I kept waiting, and now there's this version of the friendship that's dead and I'm the only one grieving it. The framing of "you were protecting yourself" doesn't capture how humiliating it feels to have cared that much more than she did.
therapist: The anger and the humiliation you're naming — that's not messy, that's the real thing, and it took courage to say it out loud. There's a particular kind of grief that comes from losing someone who's still alive, where you don't even get the clarity of a clean ending, just the slow realization that you cared in a way that wasn't matched. I want to stay with what you said about humiliation — because underneath that word, I wonder if there's a story you're telling yourself about what it means that you cared that much?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, fast speech

client: Yeah, I think the story I tell myself is something like... if I cared that much and they didn't, then I must have been foolish. Like I missed some obvious sign that I wasn't as important to them as they were to me, and everyone else probably saw it except me. It makes me feel naive, almost embarrassed to have been so open with someone who was just kind of... coasting through our friendship.
therapist: That story — that caring deeply made you foolish — is such a painful one to carry, and I want to gently challenge it: openness and investment in a friendship aren't signs of naivety, they're signs of someone who knows how to love well. The problem wasn't that you cared too much; it's that she wasn't able to meet you there, and those are very different things. What would it feel like to hold yourself as someone who was generous, rather than someone who was blind?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it, but it's hard not to feel like generosity and blindness kind of go hand in hand in this situation. Like, if I had been paying more attention, maybe I would have seen the signs earlier that she wasn't as invested as I was. It almost feels like calling myself generous is just a nicer way of saying I ignored the obvious.
therapist: There's something in the way you're saying this that sounds almost urgent, like you're working hard to close a door before something uncomfortable can come through it. I want to sit with the assumption underneath what you're describing — that noticing signs earlier would have changed the outcome — because that's actually a thought worth examining: is it possible you *did* see some signs, and chose to invest anyway, which isn't blindness but a conscious bet on someone you loved? What do you think would have had to be different for you to have pulled back sooner?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I mean... yeah, okay, maybe I did see some things and just told myself they weren't that big a deal. Like there were moments where he'd cancel plans last minute or go quiet for days and I'd just rationalize it away, tell myself everyone has their stuff going on. But I don't know if calling that a "conscious bet" makes me feel any better about it — it almost sounds like you're saying I knew and did it anyway, which feels worse somehow, not better.
therapist: The way you just said that — quickly, like you needed to get it out before sitting with it — makes me wonder if acknowledging that you *did* see the signs is landing as a kind of self-indictment, like it proves something damning about you. But there's a real difference between "I knew and did it anyway, so I'm foolish" and "I saw imperfection in someone I loved and chose to believe in them anyway, because that's what love does." Which part of that feels hardest to accept right now?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I think the hardest part is that second framing you offered — "choosing to believe in someone because that's what love does" — it almost sounds too generous, like I'm letting myself off the hook too easily. Because if I accept that, then what do I do with all the times I told my friends he was fine, that they were overreacting, and basically pushed them away defending him? I wasn't just believing in him, I was actively dismissing people who cared about me, and I don't know how that fits into the "that's what love does" story.
therapist: You're not letting yourself off the hook — you're actually doing the opposite, holding yourself accountable for something real, and that deserves to be taken seriously rather than reframed away. What you're describing — defending him to your friends, dismissing their concern — that's worth sitting with, not because it makes you foolish, but because it tells you something about how much you needed the story of him to be okay. What do you think you were protecting yourself from having to know, back then?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech
